46.14. "The Blessed One said this: 'Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is bound by both ends; the person who is bound at one end and free at the other; the person who is free from both ends; and the person who has transcended both ends. And what, monks, is the person bound by both ends? Herein, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen sensual lust. He dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen ill will. He dwells with his mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen sloth and torpor. He dwells with his mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen restlessness and remorse. He dwells with his mind obsessed by doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen doubt. This, monks, is called the person bound by both ends. And what, monks, is the person bound at one end and free at the other? Herein, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen doubt; yet he possesses the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called the person bound at one end and free at the other. And what, monks, is the person free from both ends? Herein, monks, a certain person has abandoned sensual lust, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no more subject to future arising. He has abandoned ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no more subject to future arising. This, monks, is called the person free from both ends. And what, monks, is the person who has transcended both ends? Herein, monks, a certain person is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. This, monks, is called the person who has transcended both ends. "Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having thus spoken, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. 46.15. "Then, when the night had passed, a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, it was said: "The person bound by both ends, the person bound at one end and free at the other, the person free from both ends, and the person who has transcended both ends. In what way, venerable sir, is one a person bound by both ends? In what way is one a person bound at one end and free at the other? In what way is one a person free from both ends? In what way is one a person who has transcended both ends? " 'Bhikkhu, herein a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen doubt. This, bhikkhu, is called the person bound by both ends. And how, bhikkhu, is one a person bound at one end and free at the other? Herein, bhikkhu, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen doubt; yet he possesses the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, bhikkhu, is called the person bound at one end and free at the other. And how, bhikkhu, is one a person free from both ends? Herein, bhikkhu, a certain person has abandoned sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them so that they are no more subject to future arising. This, bhikkhu, is called the person free from both ends. And how, bhikkhu, is one a person who has transcended both ends? Herein, bhikkhu, a certain person is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny for enlightenment, assured. This, bhikkhu, is called the person who has transcended both ends. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all the dharmas of a Buddha? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a dharma called ‘a bodhisattva,’ nor does he perceive a dharma called ‘the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, is there even such a dharma as a ‘bodhisattva’ which the Tathāgata has taught? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, there is no such dharma as a ‘bodhisattva’ which the Tathāgata has taught. Subhūti, if there were such a dharma as a ‘bodhisattva’ which the Tathāgata had taught, then the Tathāgata would have apprehended a self, or a being, or a soul, or a person. Rules to be Observed During *Asauca* (Impurity) in *Anuloma* Marriages: 1. During the period of impurity (*asauca*), the husband shall not engage in sexual intercourse with his wife. 2. He must refrain from performing religious rites (*karmāṇi*) until the prescribed period of purification has elapsed. 3. The husband shall maintain a state of ritual purity (*śauca*) by bathing daily and avoiding contact with those who are themselves impure. 4. He must not touch the wife during her menstrual period or while she is in a state of postpartum impurity (*sūtakā*). 5. The husband shall observe silence (*mauna*) and avoid idle talk during this time. 6. He must not consume meat, garlic, onions, or other forbidden foods. 7. He shall remain seated on the floor and avoid using beds or high seats. 8. He must not travel long distances or engage in strenuous physical labor. 9. He shall perform the necessary domestic duties himself, without delegating them to others. 10. He must not visit temples or participate in public festivals during the period of impurity. 11. He shall offer prayers and recite sacred texts (*japa*) as much as possible to purify himself. 12.
Upon the completion of the period of impurity, he must perform a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) before resuming normal activities.

46.51. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his profound wisdom, perceives that the five aggregates are all empty and thereby delivers those who suffer. Thus has the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara been praised by the Buddha Śākyamuni. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there be any sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall keep it in mind, then, should they be afflicted by fire, water, poison, swords, or bandits, they will all be delivered from such calamities. Moreover, Ānanda, if there be any sons or daughters of good family who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, shall keep it in mind, and if they should happen to fall into the hands of robbers and be about to be executed, then at that moment, by virtue of the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s name, the executioners’ weapons shall break into pieces and they shall not be killed. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there be any women who, desiring to give birth to a child, shall keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind, they shall immediately give birth to a healthy child, free from suffering. For this reason, Ānanda, you should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great compassionate power and is able to deliver sentient beings from suffering. If one wishes to offer worship to all the Buddhas of the ten directions, one should first worship the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because, Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings. Therefore, Ānanda, you should always keep the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara in mind. If there be any sons or daughters of good family who wish to practice the bodhisattva path, they should first learn and uphold the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? [[page 28-to-28]] The present work is intended as a concise introduction to the study of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the foundational treatise of the Vaibhāṣika school of Buddhist philosophy. It provides a systematic overview of the text’s structure, its historical context within the Indian Buddhist tradition, and the principal themes it addresses. By examining the *Kośa* through its doctrinal categories (*dharmas*) and its methodological approach to the analysis of consciousness, matter, and the path to liberation, this introduction aims to equip the reader with the necessary tools for a deeper engagement with the text itself. It further seeks to clarify the relationship between the *Kośa* and its primary source, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, as well as its influence on subsequent developments in Buddhist scholasticism across Asia. Through this preliminary survey, the reader will gain insight into the philosophical rigor and soteriological purpose that characterize this seminal work in the history of Buddhist thought.

--- [[page 79-to-79]] --- The Blessed One said: "Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are the four? They are: (1) the self-nature of attachment to words, (2) the self-nature of attachment to the multiplicity of things, (3) the self-nature of attachment to false discrimination, and (4) the self-nature of the perfection of ultimate reality. Mahāmati said: "What is meant by the self-nature of attachment to words? The Blessed One replied: "It refers to the habitual tendency toward the proliferation of names and signs, which arises from the beginningless past, and through which one clings to the idea that the various dharmas possess intrinsic characteristics corresponding to their verbal designations. Mahāmati asked: "What is meant by the self-nature of attachment to the multiplicity of things? The Blessed One replied: "It refers to the clinging to the notion that external objects exist as distinct entities, based on the perception of differences in form, color, and other attributes, which arises from the habit-energy of false discrimination. Mahāmati asked: "What is meant by the self-nature of attachment to false discrimination? The Blessed One replied: "It refers to the clinging to the duality of subject and object, which arises from the habit-energy of false discrimination, such that one perceives a world of external objects where none truly exist, and fails to realize that all is but the manifestation of one's own mind. Mahāmati asked: "What is meant by the self-nature of the perfection of ultimate reality? The Blessed One replied: "It refers to the realization of the non-arising of all dharmas, the absence of self-nature, and the state of being free from the dualistic grasping of existence and non-existence; it is the attainment of the Tathāgata-knowledge through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). The Blessed One further said: "Mahāmati, these four kinds of self-nature are taught to lead sentient beings to abandon their attachments and to enter into the stage of the Tathāgata."
